notes.bp: A listener in noise may need speech made clearer after capture, but enhancement should not erase speech or make the result sound unnatural.
notes.wh: Noise statistics change over time and a useful near-end method has to estimate what belongs to the noise without relying on a clean reference.
notes.naive: Use one fixed noise estimate or raise all frequencies equally and assume intelligibility will follow.
notes.ap: Estimate long-term fractile noise statistics and use them to guide near-end listening enhancement, then test the method against speech and noise conditions.
notes.mech: The paper analyzes and extends a near-end listening-enhancement method based on long-term fractile noise statistics.
notes.math: The method treats noise as a distribution over time rather than a single fixed level; enhancement is constrained by the estimated noise floor so speech structure is not indiscriminately removed.
notes.ww: The paper reports listening-enhancement results for the proposed statistical method and its extension.
notes.limits: Noise type, recordings, listeners, parameter settings, and perceptual tests limit generalization; improved quality is not identical to improved intelligibility.
notes.title: Analysis and Extension of a Near-End Listening Enhancement Method Based on Long-Term Fractile Noise Statistics

notes.bp: Sentence mode—such as a question or statement—is carried not only by words but also by prosody, and a useful model should work across languages and modalities.
notes.wh: Prosody varies with language, speaker, emotion, and recording; text alone misses timing and pitch while audio alone can miss lexical structure.
notes.naive: Predict sentence mode from text or one acoustic feature and assume the same cue works across languages.
notes.ap: Combine multimodal prosody representations and evaluate multilingual sentence-mode prediction under the actual interaction between words, voice, and language.
notes.mech: The study presents multimodal prosody modeling for multilingual sentence-mode prediction.
notes.math: Sentence mode is a joint signal: lexical content provides one constraint while pitch, timing, and energy provide another, and disagreement between them is informative rather than noise.
notes.ww: The paper reports multilingual multimodal prosody-modeling results for sentence-mode prediction.
notes.limits: Languages, labels, speaker balance, modality quality, and task definition bound the claim; sentence mode is not a complete model of intent.
notes.title: Multimodal Prosody Modeling: A Use Case for Multilingual Sentence Mode Prediction

notes.bp: A recognizer for dysarthric speech should adapt to a particular speaker even when only limited recordings are available.
notes.wh: Dysarthria changes the relation between intended words and acoustic realization; synthetic data can add coverage but can also repeat the wrong errors or sound unlike the speaker.
notes.naive: Fine-tune on a small personal set only, or add generic synthetic speech without controlling what variation it contributes.
notes.ap: Use LLM-generated transcripts to create controllable synthetic speech and personalize fine-tuning for the target speaker, then measure recognition under speaker-specific conditions.
notes.mech: The paper studies personalized fine-tuning with controllable synthetic speech for dysarthric speech recognition.
notes.math: Personalization is a data-design problem: synthetic examples are useful only when their transcript, pronunciation variation, and speaker control support the target speaker rather than dilute them.
notes.ww: The paper reports recognition results for personalized adaptation using controllable synthetic data.
notes.limits: Speaker cohort, dysarthria type, transcript generation, synthesis quality, and adaptation budget limit generalization or clinical claims.
notes.title: Personalized Fine-Tuning with Controllable Synthetic Speech from LLM-Generated Transcripts for Dysarthric Speech Recognition

notes.bp: A low-resource language needs an honest speech-recognition benchmark before claims about progress can be compared.
notes.wh: Small corpora make train/test estimates unstable, spelling and dialect choices affect labels, and a benchmark can expose gaps without solving data scarcity.
notes.naive: Report one model score on a tiny corpus and treat it as a general language capability estimate.
notes.ap: Build the Faetar speech-recognition benchmark with documented recordings, splits, transcripts, and evaluation so later systems can be compared on the same problem.
notes.mech: The paper introduces the Faetar Speech Recognition Benchmark.
notes.math: Benchmark construction is part of scientific knowledge: the dataset fixes what counts as an error and makes future improvements distinguishable from changes in collection or split.
notes.ww: The paper reports the benchmark resources and baseline recognition results for Faetar.
notes.limits: Corpus size, speakers, dialect coverage, transcription conventions, and split design bound conclusions about the wider language community.
notes.title: The Faetar Speech Recognition Benchmark

notes.bp: An audio watermark should survive ordinary processing and neural codecs while remaining detectable, otherwise it cannot support provenance or accountability in real systems.
notes.wh: Compression and generative codecs intentionally alter waveform details; a watermark can be detectable in clean audio yet disappear after the transformations people actually use.
notes.naive: Test only clean files or assume a watermark that survives one codec survives every neural codec.
notes.ap: Evaluate audio-watermarking algorithms under a broad real-world transformation suite, including neural codecs, and compare detectability and audio quality.
notes.mech: The paper provides a comprehensive real-world assessment of audio watermarking algorithms and asks whether they survive neural codecs.
notes.math: Robustness is a chain of transformations: a watermark claim is meaningful only over an explicit threat/process set, with detectability balanced against audible distortion.
notes.ww: The paper reports comparative survival and failure patterns across watermarking methods and neural codecs.
notes.limits: Algorithms, codec versions, payloads, thresholds, and attack suite bound the result; survival in tested codecs is not universal tamper resistance.
notes.title: A Comprehensive Real-World Assessment of Audio Watermarking Algorithms: Will They Survive Neural Codecs?

notes.bp: A compact system should translate simultaneous speech and produce multiple sound spots on a laptop carried in a backpack, without assuming a server or a quiet turn-taking environment.
notes.wh: Simultaneous speech translation combines overlap, latency, translation uncertainty, and spatial/audio output under tight compute and mobility constraints.
notes.naive: Wait for a complete utterance, send it to a large remote system, or treat translation and sound placement as separate problems.
notes.ap: Integrate simultaneous speech translation with compact multiple-sound-spot synthesis in a portable system and evaluate the complete interaction loop.
notes.mech: The paper presents a simultaneous speech-translation system integrated with compact multiple sound-spot synthesis on a laptop carried in a backpack.
notes.math: The system boundary is the product: recognition, translation, timing, and spatialized output must jointly meet latency and resource constraints rather than optimize isolated modules.
notes.ww: The paper reports an integrated portable-system demonstration and evaluation.
notes.limits: Language pair, overlap conditions, hardware, latency measurement, and user setting limit generalization to broad simultaneous conversation.
notes.title: Simultaneous Speech Translation Integrated Compact Multiple Sound Spot Synthesis System On A Laptop Carried Out With A Backpack

notes.bp: People use gaze and other visible cues to signal that a turn is ending or beginning, especially when noise makes audio timing unreliable.
notes.wh: Turn-taking is a coupled prediction-and-action problem: visual cues can arrive before words finish, while noise corrupts the acoustic evidence and social norms vary.
notes.naive: Predict the next turn from audio alone or treat a detected pause as a universal handoff signal.
notes.ap: Add visual cues to turn-taking prediction and test whether they make decisions more robust in noise.
notes.mech: The study evaluates visual cues for robust turn-taking prediction in noise.
notes.math: A turn is a coordination event between people, not merely a boundary in a waveform; combining channels lets one cue compensate when another is degraded.
notes.ww: The paper reports that visual cues support more robust turn-taking prediction under noisy conditions.
notes.limits: Participants, camera viewpoint, interaction task, noise type, timing labels, and model latency bound the claim; a lab cue is not a universal conversational rule.
notes.title: Visual Cues Support Robust Turn-taking Prediction in Noise

notes.bp: A speech-aware language model should follow spoken instructions and retain earlier abilities after learning new ones.
notes.wh: Instruction following can improve while unrelated skills are forgotten; speech adds recognition errors and modality-specific variation to the usual language-model tradeoff.
notes.naive: Measure only new-task accuracy or train on new instruction data and assume old abilities remain intact.
notes.ap: Use Speech-IFEval to test instruction-following behavior and quantify catastrophic forgetting across speech-aware tasks.
notes.mech: The paper introduces Speech-IFEval and evaluates instruction-following and forgetting in speech-aware language models.
notes.math: Evaluation must pair compliance with retention: a model that follows a new command by losing old behavior has shifted capability rather than simply improved it.
notes.ww: The paper reports benchmark results for spoken instruction following and catastrophic forgetting.
notes.limits: Task suite, speech recognition quality, prompts, model families, and training order bound the conclusions; benchmark retention is not proof of reliable deployment behavior.
notes.title: Speech-IFEval: Evaluating Instruction-Following and Quantifying Catastrophic Forgetting in Speech-Aware Language Models
